newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Post-holiday trade seen mixed.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Post-holiday trade seen mixed.

text.p: Soft commodity trading will gather pace this week as operators return from year-end holidays, but price movements may show a mixed trend, traders said.
London's white sugar prices could rise to test higher levels on the back of gains in New York, but cocoa may continue to battle with 900 stg a tonne on the upside.
Robusta coffee is hovering at below $1,250 a tonne, a level seen since early December, but traders said the commodity could be buoyed by renewed fund short-covering.
Sugar traders are looking forward to increased activity from early this week as market players return after the holiday.
Some see it testing higher levels, with New York March raws futures possibly targetting 11.05 or 11.06 U.S. cents a lb.
But there are forces holding it back. "There's a big wodge of producer selling around 11 cents," one said.
London's March white sugar futures closed $2.40 firmer at $311.50 a tonne on Friday.
The March LIFFE robusta coffee contract, following New York's easier trend, tumbled to re-test a life-low of $1,225 a tonne on Friday in thin volume. It closed $2 down at $1,227.
But traders said the chances of further losses seemed slim.
"I believe New York is overbought, London is oversold," said one. "Furthermore, the funds are short in London and long in New York."
"I think that (situation) will correct itself," he added.
New York's March/March arbitrage against London remained wide at a 60 cents premium.
"The premiums are getting to ridiculous levels at the moment, something that is probably going to be addressed by the ACPC," the trader added.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) is due to meet in Brazil on January 23 to discuss whether to tighten up on members' exports to boost prices.
"It would be wonderful if the ACPC could tighten the robusta quota, but we cannot see that happening without (non-member) Vietnam joining, and that is pretty unlikely," broker GNI said.
Some coffee officials and traders will gather in Vietnam next week for a trade conference at which the question of Hanoi's admission could be raised.
The direction of cocoa futures will continue to be governed by sterling's movements.
"Cocoa keeps trying to break through the 900 (stg) convincingly but it never does," one trader said.
The market hit a high of 906 stg at one stage on Friday but failed to hold above 900 level by the close as sterling's renewed strength against the dollar prompted trade profit-taking.
The contract finished Friday eight down at 896.
On the fundamental front, traders are awaiting European and U.S. grind data due to be released later this week and next week to provide new leads.
UK and Dutch markets reported sharply higher grinds in the third quarter, with the UK alone rising by 42 percent to 48,855 tonnes year-on-year.
